newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope backs Poland's NATO, EU bids - Kwasniewski.
newsitem.headline: Pope backs Poland's NATO, EU bids - Kwasniewski.

text.p: Pope John Paul, widely seen as a key influence behind the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe, gave his support on Monday to Poland's drive to join NATO and the European Union, President Aleksander Kwasniewski said.

The ex-communist head of state, speaking after he met the Pope for the first time in a 40-minute audience at the Vatican, said the Polish Pontiff's hopes for his homeland were like the culmination of a mission.
"The Pope understands very well that this question -- Poland in the European structures -- is one of the most important elements of his activity since the beginning," he told Reuters.
"This man, the Polish Pope, was the first man to say central Europe is part of a common continent," he said in English.
Poland, together with Hungary and the Czech Republic, are set to be invited by NATO in July to join the western military alliance. Warsaw is also seeking European Union membership.
"The Pope shares Poland's wish," Kwasniewski told reporters.

The 76-year-old Pope, who has retained close links with his homeland since his election in 1978, is widely credited with providing spiritual inspiration for former president Lech Walesa's Solidarity movement to overthrow communism in 1989.
Kwasniewski's November 1995 defeat of Walesa, a devout Roman Catholic, was seen as a big blow for the Pope.
Relations between the Roman Catholic Church and the Polish state have been strained in recent months after Kwasniewski signed a liberalised abortion law despite the Pope's objections.
Another thorn in their relations is the lack of progress on ratifying a bilateral treaty, or concordat, signed in 1993, which is designed to keep the state and Church separate.

The Pope and Kwasniewski exchanged polite handshakes at the start of their meeting. The atmosphere appeared warmer when Kwasniewski introduced his wife Yolanta, daughter Aleksandra and other members of his entourage after their private talks.
Chief Vatican Spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls told reporters the two men discussed Polish political and social issues.

The Pope, who visits Sarajevo next weekend on his first foreign trip of the year and is due to begin his sixth trip to Poland on May 31, had looked tired over Easter. But Kwasniewski said: "The Pope was today in very good shape."
He even joked with the president at the end of the audience. "When I come to Poland, you'll have a lot to do with me.
"I'll cause you a lot of problems," he added in a quip about security and organisational matters during his 11-day trip.
Kwasniewski replied that Poland would be ready. "Poland is happy to welcome the Holy Father," he told a news conference.
Kwasniewski's ex-communist colleagues from the ruling leftist coalition have blocked ratification of the concordat with the Vatican.
But the 42-year-old president said he believed the obstacles to ratification had been ironed out with the drafting of a new constitution, to be put to a referendum on May 25.
Asked whether he believed it could now be ratified quickly, Kwasniewski said: "I hope so."
Kwasniewski said he and the Pope had agreed that "the abortion question" should be tackled through education.
Kwasniewski was due to meet Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro later on Monday and to hold talks with Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Tuesday.
